title: Cookie attributes
summary: The `SameSite` values against each other, what `HttpOnly` and `Secure` each stop, and the two that only ever widen the blast radius. Every one of them is a line of config that fails silently.

sources.author: IETF
sources.title: draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22: Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism

cards.front: `SameSite=Strict` and `SameSite=Lax`. What does `Lax` add back, and what does it still refuse?
cards.back: `Lax` adds back cross-site top-level navigations with a safe method, so a link from another site carries the cookie. A cross-site `POST`, `fetch` or `` still goes without it.

cards.front: `SameSite=None` without `Secure`. What does the browser do with that `Set-Cookie`?
cards.back: Ignores it entirely: the spec aborts on a `SameSite=None` cookie that is not `Secure`. The header is right there in devtools and the cookie is nowhere.

cards.front: You left `SameSite` off. Which value do you get?
cards.back: It depends on the browser, which is the reason to set it. Chromium uses `Lax`; Firefox still treats an absent attribute as `None`.

cards.front: An injected script cannot read your `HttpOnly` session cookie. What can it still do with it?
cards.back: Spend it. `HttpOnly` only hides the cookie from `document.cookie`, so a same-origin `fetch` from the injected script still carries it; what the attacker loses is a copy to replay from their own machine.

cards.front: What does `Secure` actually constrain, and what does it leave open?
cards.back: Transport only: the cookie is sent only over `https:`, localhost excepted. Without `HttpOnly` it is still readable from JavaScript, so a session cookie wants both.

cards.front: What does renaming a cookie to `__Host-session` commit you to, and what do you get back?
cards.back: It commits to `Secure`, set from HTTPS, no `Domain` attribute, and `Path=/`, and a `Set-Cookie` that breaks that is dropped. In return only the exact host that set it receives it, and no path can override it.

cards.front: `Domain` on a cookie. Which direction does it move the scope, and why is that a subdomain problem in both directions?
cards.back: It only ever widens: set it and every subdomain gets the cookie, third-party hosting included. In reverse, a sibling subdomain can write a cookie scoped to the parent that the parent cannot tell from its own.

cards.front: `Max-Age` and `Expires` on the same cookie, and a cookie with neither. What happens in each case?
cards.back: `Max-Age` wins when both are set, and with neither you get a session cookie. A browser that restores tabs on launch restores those cookies too, which is how users stay logged in for weeks.
